extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, critics, and poets (especially those studying or evaluating epic poetry such as Milton's Paradise Lost)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for assessing (and composing) epic or heroic poetry, illustrated by a critical reading of Milton's Paradise Lost. Focuses on fable/plot type, character/hero role, probability, digressions, sentiments, and poetic language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable type (simple vs implex)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fable of every poem is either Simple (no change of fortune) or Implex (fortune of the chief actor changes from bad to good or good to bad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implex is generally more perfect because it better stirs the passions and surprises the reader. There are two kinds of implex: (1) rise from danger to honour (e.g., Ulysses) and (2) fall from eminent honour to misery (e.g., Oedipus, Adam and Eve). Choose the fable-type appropriate to the genre: the tragic/impl ex fall suits tragedy, but may be less proper for an heroic poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of an unhappy event for an heroic poem
rubrics_metrics.description: An unhappy or fall-from-grace fable (hero unsuccessful) is not well suited to the heroic/epic poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the tragic implex excels in tragedy, an heroic poem should avoid making its principal action end unhappily; if the epic includes a fall, the poet should attempt cures (e.g., visions of future triumph, mitigations) to restore balance and provide a satisfying plan for the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of the Hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The epic should present a clear principal actor or Hero appropriate to the poem's plan and principal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake ancillary or villainous figures for the Hero; in Paradise Lost the Messiah (not Satan) is the true Hero when the poem is judged by its principal action and chief episodes. The poet's design must support whoever is intended as Hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and plausibility of allegorical actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Particulars interwoven into the fable (especially allegorical actions) must have sufficient probability for an epic poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assigning unlikely or whimsical actions to allegorical figures (e.g., the actions of Sin and Death or the picture of Limbo of Vanity) that strain the poem's verisimilitude. Such allegories may befit Spenser or Ariosto but undermine the epic dignity expected with Homer/Virgil models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of unnecessary digressions
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic should minimize digressions that interrupt the narration; the author should let the fable proceed rather than pausing for reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle advises the poet to speak little in his own person and to let principal actors deliver much of the work. Reflections and digressions are only justified when they serve the main event (e.g., Virgil's Tenth Book reflection that clarifies the fate of Turnus). Excessive digressions (e.g., Milton's complaints, panegyrics, reflections) suspend the narrative and are liable to criticism, even if they contain beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intrusion vs. speech by characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should minimize speaking in his own person and instead throw the substance of the work into the mouths of principal actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are more elevated when they hear celebrated characters speak; assuming the character's voice can inspire the author (Tully's anecdote about Cato). Too much authorial address diminishes imitative power and can reveal the poet rather than the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments: avoid pointedness and puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments in the poem should avoid being too pointed or degenerating into puns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-pointed remarks and verbal jokes (punning) lessen dignity. Example cited: Milton's line on pigmies—'The small Infantry / Warrdon by Cranes'—is an instance of a too facetious turn that detracts from solemnity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments: avoid inappropriate heathen allusions presented as truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusions to heathen fables are acceptable when presented as fabulous, but improper when treated as truths within a divine subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent allusions to pagan fables that are not explicitly framed as fable harm the coherence of a divine or sacred subject. Where used, such classical references should be clearly signalled or subordinated to the poem's theological frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments: avoid ostentation of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem should not display an unnecessary ostentation of learning within its sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Homer and Virgil embody the learning of their times in an indirect and concealed manner, Milton is criticized for obvious excursions into free-will, predestination, and other learned topics. Learning should enrich, not parade, and should not distract from the emotional and imaginative force of the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language: avoid over-laboured, obscure, or archaic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic language should not be so laboured or obscured by old words, transpositions, and foreign idioms that it becomes unintelligible or harsh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscure diction is sometimes defended by the sublimity of the poet's ideas, but excessive archaisms and learned constructions can make the language unequal to the sentiments. Balance grandeur of conception with clarity of expression so ordinary readers can grasp lofty ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language: avoid 'jingle' and trivial verbal echoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid gratuitous jingles (obvious verbal repetitions and sound-play) that appear poor and trifling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though some ancients allowed such figures, modern polite writing generally rejects them as petty. Examples: 'And brought into the World a World of Woe' and 'Begirt th' Almighty throne / Beseeching or besieging'—such devices are viewed as weak except where rhetorically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language: avoid excessive technical terms or terms of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overload poetry with technical terms from arts and sciences (terms of art) that make abstruse matter less accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should render hard things intelligible in easy language; technical vocabulary (e.g., larboard, Doric pillars, eccentrics, trepidation, ecliptic) risks showing knowledge drawn from books rather than inspired. Keep imagery and diction comprehensible to ordinary readers and preserve the sense that poetic knowledge is innate or inspired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make abstruse subjects intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poet should make difficult or abstruse subjects intelligible through clear and elevated expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The knowledge of a poet ought to seem born with him and to be conveyed so that ordinary readers can understand. Rather than displaying erudition openly, render complexity through striking, lucid poetic means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of digressions must be justified by relevance to main action
rubrics_metrics.description: When reflections or digressions occur, they should be kept only if they are necessary to bring an incident or to elucidate an important aspect of the fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virgil's large reflection in the Tenth Book is permitted because it helps the reader remember and understand the circumstances that determine Turnus's fate; Milton's other digressions are criticized when they appear ornamental rather than serviceable to the plot.
